Prompt 1: Project setup and rules
We are going to build a data science project together, step by step. In this first stage, I want you to understand the rules of how we will work, and create 3 files in the same folder as the Python file I have open. Do not write any analysis or model code yet.

1 - rules.md
This file contains the general data science workflow rules we must follow throughout the whole project. Include at least:
- The correct order of the workflow: problem definition → data understanding → data cleaning → EDA → train/test split → preprocessing → feature engineering → modeling → evaluation → reporting
- Always split train/test BEFORE any scaling, encoding, imputation or feature selection, and fit transformers only on the training set to prevent data leakage
- Use a fixed random_state for reproducibility and stratify the split for classification problems
- Handle missing values, duplicates and outliers deliberately, and document every decision with its reason
- Prefer sklearn Pipelines / ColumnTransformer for preprocessing
- Always build a simple baseline model before trying complex models
- Use cross-validation on the training set for model selection and hyperparameter tuning; use the test set only once at the end
- Choose evaluation metrics that fit the problem (e.g. don't rely only on accuracy for imbalanced data)
- Never invent or assume numbers; every value written to the reports must come from actually running code
- After every step, update data_characteristics.md and Findings_Report.md

2 - data_characteristics.md
This file will hold the characteristics of the dataset, such as row and column count, column names and data types, missing value counts and percentages, duplicate count, target variable distribution, basic statistics, and correlation values. For now, create it with clear section headings and placeholders. We will fill it in once the dataset is loaded.

3 - Findings_Report.md
This file will hold the results and critical notes from data cleaning, data analysis and machine learning: cleaning decisions and their impact, key EDA insights, model results and comparison tables, the best model, and final conclusions. For now, create it with section headings and placeholders. We will fill it in step by step as we go.

From now on, follow rules.md in every step. After creating these files, just reply "OK" and wait for my next instruction.
Prompt 2: Data understanding (observation only)
Now we move to the data understanding stage. The dataset is demand_forecasting.csv and the target variable is Demand. Follow rules.md.

IMPORTANT: This stage is observation only. Do NOT drop, fill, encode, scale or modify the data in any way. Just analyze and document.

Write the code in my open Python file, run it, and show me the outputs. Do the following analysis:

1 - Basic structure
- Load the data, show .head(), .tail() and .sample(5)
- .shape, .info(), .dtypes
- Separate the columns into numerical, categorical, datetime and possible ID columns (e.g. columns where every value is unique)
- Flag any columns stored with the wrong type (e.g. numbers stored as strings)

2 - Statistical summary
- .describe() for numerical columns and .describe(include='object') for categorical columns
- Skewness and kurtosis for every numerical column, and flag highly skewed ones (|skew| > 1)
- Number of unique values per column; flag high-cardinality categorical columns and constant / near-constant columns

3 - Data quality
- Missing value count and percentage per column, sorted from highest to lowest
- Check whether missing values seem random or appear together in certain rows / columns
- Number of fully duplicated rows
- Suspicious values: negative values where they make no sense, impossible ranges, placeholder values like 0, -1, 999, "unknown", "?" or empty strings

4 - Outlier analysis
- For each numerical column, outlier count and percentage using the IQR method (1.5 × IQR) and the Z-score method (|z| > 3)
- Compare the two methods and note which columns have serious outlier problems

5 - Target variable analysis
- If classification: class counts and percentages, and whether the data is imbalanced
- If regression: distribution, skewness, and whether a log transform may be needed later
- Relationship of each feature with the target (correlation for numerical features, group-wise target mean / distribution for categorical features)

6 - Relationship analysis
- Pearson AND Spearman correlation matrices for numerical features; explain any big difference between the two (a sign of non-linear relationships or outliers)
- List feature pairs with |correlation| > 0.7 as multicollinearity candidates
- Calculate VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) for numerical features (on a temporary copy with missing rows excluded, without modifying the original data)
- Cramér's V for relationships between categorical features
- Mutual information scores between the features and the target, to catch non-linear relationships

After the analysis, fill in data_characteristics.md with all the real values from the outputs, using clear sections and tables. At the end of the file, add a "Key Observations & Risks" section listing the problems we will need to handle in the cleaning and preprocessing stages (e.g. columns with high missingness, skewed features, outliers, imbalance, multicollinearity, leakage suspects).

Do not write any number you did not get from running the code. When you finish, give me a short summary of the 5 most important findings.
Prompt 3: Cleaning, EDA and preprocessing
Great work. MAE is confirmed as the primary metric, with RMSE and WAPE as secondary metrics. Now we move to data cleaning, EDA and preprocessing. Follow rules.md and use the findings in data_characteristics.md.

Keep in mind the plan for the rest of the project, because this stage must prepare for it:
- Next stage: modeling (baseline + several models, TimeSeriesSplit CV, final test evaluation, saving the best model)
- After that: a FastAPI backend + a good-looking HTML frontend where the user selects a store, a product and a date, and gets a demand forecast
- Finally: running the backend and frontend
So every transformation here must be reproducible later for a single new prediction.

Create a new file called preprocessing.py, write the code there, run it and show me the outputs. Save all plots to a "figures/" folder.

FORECASTING SETUP (decide and document)
- Task: 1-day-ahead demand forecast per series. The series key is (Store ID, Product ID).
- Features available at forecast time: calendar features, planned Price / Discount / Promotion, and past values only. Treat Weather Condition, Competitor Pricing and Epidemic as known for the forecast day (assume they come from forecasts or announcements), and write that assumption clearly in Findings_Report.md.

1 - Cleaning
- Convert Date to datetime and sort by Store ID, Product ID, Date
- Create a series_id column from (Store ID, Product ID)
- Keep the Units Sold > Demand rows (27.63%) and the high-side outliers. Do not remove them, but document why (they look like genuine values or a synthetic generation rule, and removing rows would break the continuous daily series)
- Verify the integrity again after cleaning: 100 series × 760 days, no gaps

2 - Leakage handling
- Remove same-day Units Sold, Units Ordered and Inventory Level from the feature set. They may only be used as lagged values (shifted by at least 1 day within each series)
- Prove the leakage with a quick check: show the correlation of same-day Units Sold vs lag-1 Units Sold with Demand

3 - Visual EDA (save every plot, and after each one write 1–2 sentences on what it shows)
- Daily total demand over time, with epidemic days shaded
- Demand distribution (histogram + boxplot)
- Demand by Category, Weather Condition, Promotion, Discount level and Epidemic (boxplots)
- Correlation heatmap of the final numerical features
- Average demand by month and by day of week
- Investigate why Price has high mutual information (0.3406) but near-zero correlation: check whether price levels identify series or categories, and plot Price vs Demand coloured by Category. Write a conclusion.

4 - Feature engineering (all lag and rolling features must be computed per series_id and must look backward only, using shift(1) before any rolling window)
- Calendar: year, month, day of month, day of week, week of year, is_weekend, month as cyclical sin/cos
- Demand lags: lag 1, 7, 14, 28
- Demand rolling stats (shifted): rolling mean 7/14/28, rolling std 7
- Lagged operational values: Units Sold lag 1 and 7, Units Ordered lag 1, Inventory Level lag 1
- Price features: price_gap = Price − Competitor Pricing and price_ratio = Price / Competitor Pricing. Then drop Competitor Pricing to remove the multicollinearity (VIF ≈ 21.7)
- Epidemic context: the epidemic flag plus the number of epidemic days in the past 7 days (shifted)
- Drop the redundant columns: Region (determined by Store ID) and Seasonality (determined by month)
- Drop the first 28 days of each series, where the lags are NaN, and record how many rows were removed

5 - Chronological train/test split
- Use the final 120 days as the test set and everything before as the training set. NO random split.
- Check and report that the test period includes both epidemic and non-epidemic days. If it does not, adjust the window and explain why
- Report the date ranges, row counts and demand mean for train and test

6 - Preprocessing (fit ONLY on the training set)
- Build a sklearn ColumnTransformer: one-hot encode Store ID, Category and Weather Condition; target-free ordinal or one-hot encoding for Product ID; scale the numerical features with StandardScaler (needed for linear models; trees will ignore it)
- Do NOT fit anything on the test set. Do not save a fitted transformer yet: it will go inside the model pipeline in the next stage

7 - Save the outputs for the next stages
- data/train.csv and data/test.csv (engineered, unscaled, including Date, series_id and the target)
- data/history.csv: the full cleaned daily history with the raw columns, needed later by the API to compute lag features for a new prediction
- feature_config.json: target name, the exact feature list split into numerical / categorical, the series key, the lag and rolling settings, the split date and the forecasting assumptions

8 - Update the reports
- data_characteristics.md: fill in section 11 (Train/Test Split Summary), add every change to the Change Log table (rows and columns before/after), and list the final feature set
- Findings_Report.md: add a "Data Cleaning & Preprocessing" section and an "EDA Insights" section with every decision and its reason, the leakage proof, the Price/MI conclusion, the forecasting assumptions, and references to the saved figures

Do not write any number you did not get from running the code. When you finish, give me a short summary: the final feature count, the train/test sizes and date ranges, and the 5 most important EDA insights.
Prompt 4: Modeling
Great work. Now we move to the modeling stage. Follow rules.md and use everything in data_characteristics.md and Findings_Report.md.

From now on, all the critical findings and modeling documentation will also be collected in a new file called project_documentation.md. This is the single complete document of the project (details in step 9).

Create a new file called modeling.py, write the code there, run it and show me the outputs. Import add_features / build_preprocessor from preprocessing.py and read every setting from feature_config.json. Do not hard-code feature lists. Save the plots to figures/, continuing the numbering (08_, 09_, ...).

1 - Time-series cross-validation setup
- Load data/train.csv and data/test.csv. Use the test set ONLY in step 6.
- Build a cross-validation splitter on UNIQUE DATES, not on rows, so all 100 series of a day always stay in the same fold: an expanding-window TimeSeriesSplit with 5 folds over the training dates. Print the date range of every fold.
- Metrics for every evaluation: MAE (primary), RMSE, WAPE and R². Also record the training time.

2 - Baselines (no training, evaluated on the same CV folds)
- Naive: prediction = demand_lag_1
- Seasonal naive: prediction = demand_lag_7
- Moving average: prediction = demand_roll_mean_7
- The best baseline is the bar every model must beat

3 - Model comparison (every model inside a Pipeline with build_preprocessor(), so CV stays leak-free)
- Linear Regression, Ridge, Lasso
- Random Forest (keep it reasonably fast, e.g. limited n_estimators / max_depth, n_jobs=-1)
- HistGradientBoostingRegressor
- LightGBM and XGBoost (install them if they are missing)
- Use random_state=42 everywhere
- Report a table with MAE / RMSE / WAPE / R² (mean ± std across folds) and training time, sorted by MAE

4 - Experiments on the best model
- Target transform: compare the raw target vs sqrt(Demand) using TransformedTargetRegressor (the log transform was rejected in Stage 2). Keep whichever has lower CV MAE.
- Price ablation: train the best model WITH and WITHOUT the price features (Price, price_gap, price_ratio) and report both CV scores. This shows how much of the performance depends on the possible Price leakage.
- Optional feature: price relative to the series' own past (Price / shifted 28-day rolling mean of Price per series). Add it to add_features() and feature_config.json ONLY if it improves CV MAE, and document the result either way.

5 - Hyperparameter tuning
- Tune the best model with RandomizedSearchCV (or Optuna) using the date-based time-series splitter, scoring = neg MAE, around 30 iterations
- Report the search space, the best parameters, the best CV MAE and the improvement over the untuned model

6 - Final evaluation (test set used ONCE)
- Fit the final pipeline on the full training set and evaluate it on the test set
- Compare it with the best baseline on the same test set and report the % improvement in MAE
- Also report the final test results without the price features, so the honest "no-Price" performance is visible

7 - Error analysis and interpretation
- Test MAE broken down by: epidemic vs non-epidemic days, Category, Store ID, and the 5 best / 5 worst series
- Plots: actual vs predicted over the test period for 3 example series (with epidemic days shaded), a residual distribution, predicted vs actual scatter, and daily total actual vs predicted demand
- Feature importance: the model's built-in importance plus permutation importance on the test set (top 20 features, plotted)
- Check for bias: mean residual overall and on epidemic days (is the model systematically over- or under-forecasting?)

8 - Saving for deployment (needed for the FastAPI app in the next stage)
- Save models/demand_model_eval.joblib: the full pipeline trained on the training set only (used for the reported test scores)
- Refit the same pipeline with the same parameters on train + test, and save it as models/demand_model.joblib for deployment. Document why.
- Create predict.py with a function:
  predict_demand(store_id, product_id, date, price, discount, promotion, weather_condition=None, competitor_pricing=None, epidemic=None)
  It loads the model + feature_config.json + data/history.csv, rebuilds all lag/rolling features from history using add_features(), and returns the prediction. Supported dates: any date inside the history (backtest mode, also returning the actual demand) and the next day after the last history date (2024-01-31, true forecast mode). Return a clear error for unsupported dates or unknown store/product pairs.
- Solve the missing-inputs gap: if weather_condition, competitor_pricing or epidemic is not provided, fill them with documented defaults: the most frequent weather for that store's region in that calendar month, competitor pricing from the series' last known price_ratio applied to the given price, and epidemic = the last known value. Also make the defaults for Price / Discount / Promotion available as the series' last known values, so the frontend can pre-fill the form.
- Save models/model_metadata.json: model name, best parameters, feature list, CV and test metrics (with and without price), training date ranges, last history date, valid stores, valid store-product pairs with their category, valid weather values, and the default rules
- Consistency check: run predict_demand() with demand_model_eval.joblib on 5 random test rows and confirm the predictions match the modeling.py test predictions exactly

9 - Documentation
- Findings_Report.md: fill in sections 5, 6 and 7 (baseline, model comparison table, tuning, final test evaluation, error analysis, feature importance, conclusions, limitations, next steps)
- data_characteristics.md: add the modeling stage to the Change Log if any feature was added
- Create project_documentation.md, the single complete document of the project:
  1. Project overview and business goal
  2. Dataset summary
  3. Critical findings (leakage, epidemic regime, Simpson's paradox in Price, redundant features, structural oddities)
  4. Forecasting setup and assumptions
  5. Cleaning and preprocessing decisions
  6. Modeling: baselines, CV method, model comparison table, experiments, tuning, final test results, with vs without Price
  7. Error analysis and feature importance, with links to the figures
  8. Deployment artifacts: what each file in models/ and data/ is, and how to call predict_demand() with an example
  9. Limitations, risks and next steps

Do not write any number you did not get from running the code. When you finish, give me a short summary: the best baseline vs the best model on the test set, the CV comparison table, the with/without Price result, the 3 most important features, and the predict_demand() consistency check result.
Prompt 5: FastAPI backend, HTML frontend, and running the app
Excellent work. The modeling stage is complete. Now we build and run the final product: a FastAPI backend and a good-looking HTML frontend on top of predict.py. Follow rules.md. Reuse predict.py, preprocessing.py, feature_config.json and models/model_metadata.json. Do NOT duplicate the feature logic, and do NOT hard-code any metric or list in the code: read them from model_metadata.json.

PART 1 - FastAPI backend (backend/main.py)
- Load models/demand_model.joblib, the metadata and data/history.csv ONCE at startup (lifespan), not on every request
- Enable CORS for the frontend origin (http://localhost:5500 and http://127.0.0.1:5500)
- Endpoints:
  - GET /health → status, model name, last history date, forecast date
  - GET /metadata → model name, CV and test metrics, improvement vs baseline, top drivers, assumptions, supported date range
  - GET /series → stores, and for each store its products with their category (from the 100 valid store-product pairs)
  - GET /defaults?store_id=&product_id=&date= → the pre-fill values from get_input_defaults() (discount, promotion, weather, epidemic) and which rule produced each one
  - POST /predict → body: store_id, product_id, date, and optional discount, promotion, weather_condition, epidemic. Returns: prediction (rounded and raw), mode (backtest / forecast), actual demand and error if backtest, the inputs used, which inputs came from defaults, and a typical error range (prediction ± test MAE from the metadata)
  - GET /history?store_id=&product_id=&end_date=&days=60 → actual daily demand for the chart, with epidemic flags
  - GET /backtest?store_id=&product_id=&start=&end= → predicted vs actual for a date range (max 120 days), computed efficiently in one batch, not by calling predict_demand() in a loop; also return the MAE for that range
- Validation with Pydantic: discount must be one of the values seen in history (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25), promotion and epidemic 0/1, weather must be a valid value, date format YYYY-MM-DD. Convert PredictionError into a clear 400 response, so the server never returns a 500 for user errors
- Add a short description to every endpoint so the Swagger docs at /docs look clean
- Create requirements.txt for the whole project

PART 2 - Frontend (frontend/index.html, a single self-contained file)
- A modern, polished dashboard design: dark theme, clean typography, cards with soft shadows, smooth transitions, fully responsive. You can use Tailwind CSS and Chart.js from a CDN
- Header: project title + a small model card loaded from /metadata (model name, test MAE, "19.64% better than baseline" read from the metadata, not hard-coded)
- Forecast form:
  - Store dropdown → Product dropdown filtered by store, showing the category (e.g. "P0001 · Electronics")
  - Date picker limited to the supported range, with a badge that switches automatically between "Backtest" (dates inside history) and "Forecast" (2024-01-31)
  - Discount, Promotion toggle, Weather and Epidemic toggle, pre-filled automatically from /defaults whenever store, product or date changes. Mark pre-filled fields with a small "default" tag that disappears when the user edits the field
  - Do not show Price inputs (the model does not use price). Add a small info tooltip explaining that price was removed due to leakage
  - A Predict button with a loading state
- Result card:
  - A big predicted demand number with the typical error range (± MAE)
  - In backtest mode: the actual demand, the error and an accuracy indicator
  - The inputs used, with the defaulted ones highlighted
- Chart (Chart.js): the last 60 days of actual demand for the selected series with epidemic days shaded, the backtest predictions as a second line, and the new prediction as a highlighted point
- A "Backtest a period" section: choose a date range, show predicted vs actual on a chart, plus the MAE for that range
- An "About the model" section: top drivers, the main assumptions (weather and epidemic assumed known), the known weak spots (slight under-forecast, post-epidemic recovery), and the 1-day-ahead limitation, all loaded from /metadata
- Friendly error messages as toasts (e.g. unsupported date), never raw JSON or a blank screen
- Keep the API base URL in a single constant at the top of the script

PART 3 - Tests
- tests/test_api.py with FastAPI TestClient: health, series, defaults, a forecast prediction, a backtest prediction, and invalid inputs (unknown store, invalid date, invalid discount) returning 400/422
- Consistency test: the /predict result for 3 backtest rows must exactly match predict_demand() with the same model and inputs
- Run the tests and show the results

PART 4 - Run everything
- Install the requirements if needed
- Start the backend: uvicorn backend.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --reload (in the background, so it keeps running)
- Start the frontend: python -m http.server 5500 inside the frontend folder (in the background)
- Smoke test the running services with curl: /health, /series, /defaults, /predict in forecast mode (2024-01-31), /predict in backtest mode (e.g. 2023-12-01) and one invalid request. Show the responses
- Confirm that http://localhost:8000/docs and http://localhost:5500 both load
- If anything fails, fix it and re-run until everything works

PART 5 - Documentation
- README.md: project summary, folder structure, how to install and run the backend and frontend, the API endpoints with example requests and responses, and screenshots placeholders
- project_documentation.md: add a section "10. Application (API & Frontend)" with the architecture (frontend → FastAPI → predict.py → model + history), the endpoint table, how defaults work, the test results and how to run it
- Findings_Report.md: add the deployment notes and the final status to the Conclusions

Do not write any number you did not get from running the code or reading the metadata. When you finish, give me a short summary: the endpoints, the test results, the curl smoke test results, and the two URLs to open in the browser.
